title: Short Stuff: Saturn's Rings
summary: Short Stuff episode on Saturn's rings, based on a HowStuffWorks article by Ian O'Neil. The hosts describe how NASA's Cassini mission (launched 1997, entered Saturn orbit 2004) burned up the probe at end of mission and flew orbits through the gap between Saturn and its inner ring. Cassini found a rain of particles falling from the rings into Saturn's atmosphere. Using gravitational tugs on the spacecraft to measure ring mass, scientists estimated the rings are young, roughly 100 to 110 million years old, rather than as old as Saturn (about 4.5 billion years). They also discuss that the rings will dissolve in about 100 million years, the atmospheric flows that complicated the mass calculations, and theories that the rings came from an icy comet or moon torn apart by Saturn's gravity. Josh promises a full episode on Saturn.
topics: Saturn gravity measurement of ring mass

segments.title: Opening and introduction to Saturn's rings
segments.summary: Hosts introduce the topic, crediting Ian O'Neil's HowStuffWorks article, and say Saturn's rings will disappear in about 100 million years and are younger than thought.

segments.title: Cassini mission background and probe disposal
segments.summary: Cassini was launched by NASA and ESA in 1997 and entered Saturn orbit in 2004. Its probe was burned up in the atmosphere, not crashed on a moon, to avoid contaminating possibly habitable moons with Earth germs.

segments.title: Cassini's ring-gap flyovers and falling ring material
segments.summary: Cassini flew orbits through the gap between Saturn and its innermost ring, expecting empty space but finding a rain of particles falling from the rings into Saturn's atmosphere, which implied the rings are slowly dissolving.

segments.title: Ring lifespan of about 100 million years
segments.summary: The hosts explain the rings have about 100 million years left, which is short compared with Saturn's roughly four-billion-year age.

segments.title: Rain rate of ring particles
segments.summary: Josh mentions a rate of ten tons of material raining per second and converts the figure to kilograms, noting it is a large amount that still takes about 100 million years to dissolve the rings.

segments.title: Weighing the rings with spacecraft gravity measurements
segments.summary: Scientists used the gravitational pull of the rings and moons on Cassini's trajectory, detecting tiny acceleration changes, to calculate the rings' mass. Less mass suggests younger rings.
topics: Saturn gravity measurement of ring mass

segments.title: Mass estimate discrepancy and atmospheric flows
segments.summary: The initial mass predictions did not match the measurements. Scientists found that large flows in Saturn's equatorial atmosphere, about 6,000 miles deep and about four percent slower than the upper clouds, were altering the spacecraft's path.
topics: Saturn gravity measurement of ring mass

segments.title: Revised ring age estimate
segments.summary: Density wave measurements and the lower mass suggested the rings are lightweight and bright with little rocky material, so they are young, estimated at 100 to 110 million years. Earlier estimates ranged from 4.5 billion years down to about 30 million.

segments.title: Origin theories and future Saturn episode
segments.summary: Possible origins include an icy comet or moon pulled apart by Saturn's gravity. Josh says a full Saturn episode is coming, and Chuck notes a planet could form rings again in future.

segments.title: Sign-off
segments.summary: The hosts wrap up the short episode and the iHeartRadio credit is read.
